question: In a Mixture of Experts (MoE) transformer layer, which component of a dense transformer block does the set of experts replace?
options: The multi-head self-attention sublayer that mixes information across tokens
The token embedding table at the input of the network
The dense feed-forward network (FFN/MLP) of the block
The final LayerNorm and the unembedding projection to the vocabulary
explanation: An MoE layer replaces the single dense feed-forward network of a transformer block with N expert FFNs plus a router. Attention is left unchanged. Each expert is itself a small FFN (for example a SwiGLU), which is why the dense FFN is the natural thing to swap out.

question: DeepSeek-V3 is described as having 671B parameters but activating only about 37B per token. What does this illustrate about Mixture of Experts models?
options: MoE gives a very large total parameter count at the inference cost of a much smaller model
MoE compresses all 671B parameters into a 37B low-rank form when the model is loaded
Only 37B parameters are ever trained; the remaining experts are frozen after initialization
The 37B are the attention weights, while the other 634B are embedding tables looked up per token
explanation: All 671B parameters are stored and trained, but each token is routed through only a small subset of experts totalling about 37B parameters. That is how frontier models get huge capacity at manageable per-token compute. Nothing is compressed or frozen; the experts just sit idle for tokens that are not routed to them.

section: 1. Intuition: more parameters, same compute per token
question: In a dense transformer, why do the parameter count and per-token FLOPs of the feed-forward network rise together?
options: Because the FFN's FLOPs depend only on sequence length, which grows with model size
Because each token uses a different random subset of FFN weights, sized to the layer width
Because larger FFNs require proportionally more attention heads to feed them inputs
Every token flows through the same FFN, so a bigger FFN costs more for every token
explanation: In a dense model each token passes through the one shared FFN, so every extra FFN parameter is used, and paid for in FLOPs, by every token. MoE breaks this coupling by letting each token use only some experts. The distractor about random subsets describes neither dense FFNs nor MoE.

section: 1. Intuition: more parameters, same compute per token
question: In a Mixture of Experts layer, what does the router (gating network) do for each token?
options: Averages the outputs of all N experts with equal weights so every expert sees each token
Scores every expert and selects the top-k experts that will process that token
Assigns tokens to experts in round-robin order so each expert gets an equal share
Picks which attention heads the token should attend with in the following layer
explanation: The router is a small learned network that produces a score for every expert; the top-k scoring experts are the only ones evaluated for that token, and their outputs are blended with gate weights. Running all experts equally would remove the compute saving, and round-robin assignment would not be learned.

section: 1. Intuition: more parameters, same compute per token
question: With a Mixture of Experts layer of N experts and top-k routing, how do total parameters and per-token FLOPs scale?
options: Both total parameters and per-token FLOPs scale linearly with N, as in a wider dense FFN
Total parameters scale with N, while per-token FLOPs stay close to k dense FFN passes
Total parameters stay constant while per-token FLOPs drop by a factor of N/k
Total parameters scale with k and per-token FLOPs scale with N, since every expert is scored and run
explanation: All N experts are stored, so parameters grow with N, but each token only touches k of them, so per-token compute is roughly k FFN passes regardless of N. This is the whole point of MoE: capacity grows without proportional compute. The tempting 'both scale with N' answer describes a dense model made N times wider.

section: 1. Intuition: more parameters, same compute per token
question: What is meant by 'sparse activation' in a Mixture of Experts model?
options: Most weights inside each expert are exactly zero after magnitude pruning during training
Activations are stored in a sparse tensor format such as CSR to save GPU memory
Only a sparse random subset of the tokens in each batch is processed at every layer
For any given token, most of the network's expert parameters are idle and not computed
explanation: Sparse activation means each token activates only its top-k experts, so most experts do no work for that token. It is not weight pruning or a sparse storage format; the experts themselves are ordinary dense FFNs. Every token is still processed, just by a few experts.

section: 1. Intuition: more parameters, same compute per token
question: What is the intuitive reason a Mixture of Experts can outperform a dense FFN of similar per-token compute?
options: Experts can specialize (code, prose, arithmetic) and the router sends each token to the most useful ones
Each expert sees every token in the batch, so each one is effectively trained on k times more data overall
Experts share all their weights through tying, which acts as a strong regularizer during training
The router replaces the attention sublayer, so the saved compute can be spent on a larger FFN
explanation: A dense FFN must be a jack-of-all-trades, while separate experts can specialize on different kinds of tokens, and the learned router directs each token to the specialists most useful for it. Experts do not see every token and do not share weights, which is exactly what makes them specialists.

section: 1. Intuition: more parameters, same compute per token
question: Mixture of Experts is described as trading memory for capacity. What exactly is traded?
options: Less memory is used per expert in exchange for slower inference, since experts are paged in on demand
Activation memory is traded for fewer parameters, because each expert recomputes its inputs
More stored parameters (memory) buy more capacity without proportionally more per-token compute
Optimizer state is discarded for routed experts in exchange for being able to store more of them
explanation: MoE must hold all N experts' parameters in memory, but each token only computes through k of them. So the cost moves from FLOPs to memory: you pay in stored parameters and get more capacity (knowledge the model can hold) at roughly constant compute per token.

question: In MoE routing $\mathbf{p} = \operatorname{softmax}(W_r\mathbf{x})$, what are the shape of the router weight $W_r$ and the meaning of $p_i$, for token vector $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^C$ and N experts?
options: $W_r\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times C}$; $p_i$ is the output activation of expert $i$ at channel $i$
$W_r\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$; $p_i$ is the load on expert $i$ in the batch
$W_r\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C}$; $p_i$ is the router's affinity (probability) for expert $i$
$W_r\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times N}$ applied after the experts; $p_i$ is expert $i$'s training loss
explanation: The router maps a C-dimensional token vector to N scores, so $W_r$ is $N\times C$, and the softmax turns those scores into a probability vector over experts. $p_i$ is how strongly the router favours expert $i$ for this token. The router runs before the experts, not after, and it does not measure batch load.

question: After selecting the top-k experts $\mathcal{T}$ in an MoE layer, how are the gate weights $g_i$ computed?
options: $g_i = p_i / \sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}} p_j$, renormalizing the kept probabilities to sum to 1
$g_i = p_i$, using the raw softmax probabilities unchanged so the kept gates sum to 1
$g_i = 1/k$ for every selected expert, ignoring the router's probabilities entirely
$g_i = \operatorname{softmax}(p)_i$ applied a second time over all N experts, then masked to the top-k
explanation: The top-k probabilities are divided by their own sum so the k gates form a proper weighted average. Raw $p_i$ would sum to less than 1, shrinking the output, and uniform $1/k$ would throw away the router's confidence information.

question: What is the output of an MoE layer for a token with selected expert set $\mathcal{T}$ and gates $g_i$?
options: $\mathbf{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} p_i\,E_i(\mathbf{x})$, a probability-weighted sum over all N experts
$\mathbf{y} = \max_{i\in\mathcal{T}} E_i(\mathbf{x})$, the elementwise maximum over the selected experts
$\mathbf{y} = E_{\text{argmax}}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \sum_i g_i$, the top expert scaled by the total kept gate
$\mathbf{y} = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} g_i\,E_i(\mathbf{x})$, a gate-weighted sum over the selected experts
explanation: Only the experts in $\mathcal{T}$ are evaluated and their outputs are blended with the renormalized gates. Summing over all N experts would require running every expert, which destroys the compute saving that defines MoE.

question: Where does the compute saving of a Mixture of Experts layer come from?
options: The router matmul replaces the FFN matmul, which is the expensive part of each block
Experts not in the token's top-k set are never evaluated for that token
Experts are evaluated at lower precision (FP8) than a dense FFN would be
Each expert is evaluated on only half its input dimensions, chosen by the router
explanation: The saving is simply that unselected experts do no work for a given token. The router is a tiny extra matmul, not a replacement for the FFN, and experts run at normal precision on the full input.

question: How many experts does each token use in Switch Transformers versus Mixtral and DeepSeek?
options: Switch uses top-2 blended by gates; Mixtral and DeepSeek use top-1 to cut communication
Switch uses top-1 (one expert); Mixtral and DeepSeek use top-2, blended by their gates
All three use top-8 routing, with gates renormalized over the eight selected experts
Switch evaluates all experts with soft gates; Mixtral and DeepSeek use hard top-1 selection
explanation: Switch Transformers introduced k = 1 routing, so each token hits exactly one expert. Mixtral and DeepSeek use k = 2 in this description, with the two expert outputs blended by their renormalized gates.

question: What is 'router collapse' in Mixture of Experts training?
options: The router's softmax outputs become exactly uniform, so every token is routed to a random expert
All experts converge to identical weights, so the router's choice no longer matters for the layer output
The router logits overflow in low precision and become NaN, which then spreads to every expert
A rich-get-richer loop where a few experts get most tokens and the rest are never selected or trained
explanation: Experts chosen slightly more often early get more gradient, improve faster, and get chosen even more. The endpoint is a handful of overworked experts and many dead ones. Uniform routing is the opposite of collapse, and identical experts is a different (redundancy) problem.

question: Besides wasting parameters, why is router collapse especially harmful when experts are sharded across devices (expert parallelism)?
options: One GPU holding the popular experts is swamped while the others sit idle
It causes the gradient all-reduce across the data-parallel ranks to deadlock
It forces every GPU to hold a full replica of every expert's weights
It doubles the size of the KV cache on the device that hosts the router
explanation: With expert parallelism each GPU holds a subset of experts, so if tokens pile onto a few experts, the device holding them does most of the work while others idle. That load imbalance wrecks throughput. It does not change the KV cache or force replication.

question: In the Switch Transformers auxiliary load-balance loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = N\sum_i f_i P_i$, what are $f_i$ and $P_i$?
options: $f_i$ is the mean router probability for expert $i$ (soft); $P_i$ is the fraction of tokens routed to it (hard)
$f_i$ is expert $i$'s share of layer FLOPs; $P_i$ is its share of the layer's parameter count
$f_i$ is the fraction of tokens routed to expert $i$ (hard); $P_i$ is its mean router probability (soft)
$f_i$ is expert $i$'s per-token loss; $P_i$ is the norm of its gradient averaged over the batch
explanation: $f_i$ counts how many tokens actually went to expert $i$ (a non-differentiable fraction from the top-k choice), and $P_i$ averages the router's softmax probability for expert $i$ over the batch (differentiable). Swapping them is the tempting mistake; the hard count is $f$ and the soft average is $P$.

question: What are the minimum and maximum values of the aux loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = N\sum_i f_i P_i$ and when do they occur?
options: Minimum 0 when routing is perfectly uniform; maximum 1 when everything goes to one expert
Minimum N when routing is perfectly uniform; maximum N squared when all tokens hit one expert
Minimum 1 when routing is perfectly uniform; maximum N when everything goes to one expert
Minimum 1 when everything goes to one expert; maximum N when routing is perfectly uniform
explanation: With $f_i = P_i = 1/N$, $N\cdot N\cdot(1/N)(1/N) = 1$. With all mass on one expert, $N\cdot 1\cdot 1 = N$. The N prefactor is what normalizes the balanced value to exactly 1 rather than 1/N or 0.

question: In the auxiliary load-balance loss, through which quantity do gradients flow to the router?
options: Through $P_i$, the mean router probability, which is differentiable
Through $f_i$, the hard per-expert token count taken from the top-k indices
Through the top-k index selection, using a straight-through estimator
Through the expert outputs $E_i(\mathbf{x})$ only, never through the router
explanation: $f_i$ comes from a discrete top-k choice and has no useful gradient, so it is treated as a constant. $P_i$ is a mean of softmax probabilities, so its gradient nudges the router to raise probability on under-used experts. The top-k selection itself is not backpropagated through.

question: How is the auxiliary load-balance loss combined with the language-modeling loss during MoE training?
options: The aux loss replaces the LM loss for the first epoch, then training switches back to LM only
Total loss is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}} \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}$, so imbalance scales the LM gradient
The aux loss is computed only at evaluation time and used to pick which experts to keep
Total loss is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}} + \alpha\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}$ with a small $\alpha$
explanation: The aux loss is added to the LM loss with a small weight $\alpha$ so it encourages balance without dominating the main objective. It is a training regularizer, not an evaluation-time tool or a multiplicative factor.

question: Intuitively, what does the aux loss $N\sum_i f_i P_i$ penalize?
options: Experts whose outputs have large norms, since those dominate the gate-weighted sum of experts
Putting many tokens (high f_i) on experts the router is already confident about (high P_i)
Tokens whose router probabilities are close to uniform, pushing the router to be confident
Experts that receive no tokens at all, by adding a large constant penalty for each dead expert
explanation: Each term multiplies how loaded an expert is by how much probability the router gives it, so the sum is large exactly when the favoured experts are also overloaded. Minimizing it lowers probability on overloaded experts and raises it on under-used ones. It does not look at output norms.

question: Why did DeepSeek-V3 look for an alternative to the auxiliary load-balance loss?
options: The aux loss cannot be computed with top-2 routing, only with Switch-style top-1 routing
The aux loss gradient competes with the language-modeling loss and can slightly hurt quality
The aux loss requires a full extra forward pass through all experts at every training step
The aux loss drives every expert toward identical weights, which removes their specialization
explanation: The aux loss adds a gradient term that pulls on the router in a direction other than lowering LM loss, which can cost a little quality. DeepSeek-V3's aux-loss-free method balances load without adding any loss gradient.

question: How does DeepSeek-V3's auxiliary-loss-free load balancing work?
options: A per-expert bias is added to the gate weights that blend expert outputs, and it is learned by gradient descent
Tokens routed to an overloaded expert are randomly reassigned to an underloaded one after top-k selection
The number of experts is increased during training whenever one expert's load exceeds a fixed threshold
A per-expert bias, used only in top-k selection, is lowered for overloaded and raised for underloaded experts
explanation: A bias $b_i$ shifts which experts win top-k selection but is not used in the gate weights, and it is updated by a simple rule after each step rather than by a loss gradient. Because balance comes from the selection bias, it does not pull on the LM objective. Adding the bias to the gates would change the outputs, which the method avoids.

question: In DeepSeek-V3's aux-loss-free balancing, is the per-expert bias used in the gate weights that blend expert outputs?
options: No; it affects only which experts are selected, not the gate weights
Yes; it is added to both the selection scores and the blending gates
Yes; it replaces the softmax gates entirely once training has warmed up
No; it is added to the expert outputs after they have been blended
explanation: The bias only shifts the top-k selection scores. The gates that weight the chosen experts' outputs still come from the unbiased router scores, so the bias changes routing without distorting the output mixture.

question: Which load-balancing method is implemented in the course's llmre.model.moe code, and how is DeepSeek-V3's bias trick classified?
options: The DeepSeek-V3 bias trick is implemented; the Switch aux loss is labelled INFERENCE/SPECULATION
Neither is implemented; both are described only as REASONABLE INDUSTRY PRACTICE without published details
The Switch-style aux loss is implemented; the bias trick is PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED in the DeepSeek-V3 report
Both are implemented and combined in the default config, with the bias trick switched on after warmup
explanation: The course code uses the classic auxiliary loss, while the aux-loss-free bias balancing is documented in the DeepSeek-V3 technical report and labelled PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED. It is described, not implemented, in the codebase.

question: What are 'shared experts' in DeepSeekMoE?
options: Experts whose weights are tied and shared across all layers of the network in order to save memory
Routed experts that two different tokens are allowed to use at the same time in one batch
One or more FFNs that are always active for every token in addition to the routed top-k experts
Experts shared between the encoder and the decoder stacks so both learn the same features
explanation: Shared experts bypass the router and process every token, while the routed experts handle the top-k selection on top. They are not cross-layer weight sharing; the 'shared' refers to being used by all tokens.

question: What is the motivation for adding always-on shared experts in DeepSeekMoE?
options: They capture common knowledge (syntax, frequent patterns) so routed experts need not relearn it and can specialize
They guarantee each token uses exactly one routed expert, which removes the need to renormalize the top-k gate weights
They reduce memory by replacing half of the routed experts with a single larger always-on network
They remove the need for any load balancing, because every token already has a guaranteed expert to use
explanation: Knowledge common to nearly all tokens would otherwise be duplicated in many routed experts, wasting capacity. Dedicating shared experts to that common case frees routed experts to specialize. Load balancing is still needed for the routed experts.

question: With shared experts, what is the MoE output for a token?
options: $\mathbf{y} = \sum_s E^{\text{shared}}_s(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} g_i E_i(\mathbf{x})$
$\mathbf{y} = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} g_i E_i(\mathbf{x})$, with shared experts used only in the router
$\mathbf{y} = \tfrac12\sum_s E^{\text{shared}}_s(\mathbf{x})$ only, routed experts used for training
$\mathbf{y} = \sum_s E^{\text{shared}}_s(\mathbf{x}) + \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} g_i E_i(\mathbf{x})$
explanation: The always-on shared expert outputs (ungated) are added to the gate-weighted sum of the routed top-k experts. It is a sum, not a product, and the shared experts contribute directly to the output, not to routing.

question: What are 'fine-grained' experts in DeepSeekMoE and what do they buy?
options: Experts that each operate on a separate slice of channels of the hidden vector, like a grouped convolution
Many small experts instead of a few large ones, giving the router more combinations at the same parameter count
Experts trained at higher numerical precision than the rest of the model so they can capture finer detail
A few very large experts that each cover one whole domain, such as source code, mathematics or natural-language prose
explanation: Splitting capacity into many smaller experts lets the router combine them in many more ways for the same total parameters, enabling finer specialization. It is not per-channel processing or a precision change.

question: In an MoE layer with N = 4 and k = 2, a token's softmax router probabilities are (0.6381, 0.2347, 0.0954, 0.0318). What happens to experts 2 and 3 for this token?
options: They run with gates 0.0954 and 0.0318, so their contribution to the output is small but nonzero
They are never evaluated; only experts 0 and 1 run, with gates about 0.73 and 0.27
They run on the token, but their outputs are discarded before the gate-weighted sum is taken
They receive the token on the next step instead, once experts 0 and 1 have been freed up
explanation: Top-2 selects experts 0 and 1; renormalizing 0.6381 and 0.2347 by their sum 0.8728 gives gates 0.7311 and 0.2689. Experts 2 and 3 are skipped entirely, which is where the compute saving comes from; running them and discarding the output would waste that saving.

question: How does the from-scratch MoE forward reshape tensors before routing?
options: It routes each sequence as a whole, producing (B, N) probabilities so all tokens of one sequence share the same experts
It transposes to (C, B, T) so that each channel of the hidden vector independently picks its own expert
It keeps (B, T, C) and computes (B, T, N, C) outputs for all experts, then masks the unselected ones
It flattens (B, T, C) to (BT, C), routes to (BT, N) probabilities, then reshapes the output back to (B, T, C)
explanation: Routing is per token, so the batch and time axes are merged into one list of N_tok tokens; the router produces one N-way probability vector per token. After dispatch and combination the output is viewed back to (B, T, C). Computing all experts' outputs for every token would defeat the sparsity.

question: In the from-scratch MoE, what architecture is each expert?
options: A SwiGLU feed-forward block from lesson 12.2
A single linear layer with no activation function
A single self-attention head with its own projections
A GELU two-layer MLP whose weights are shared with the router
explanation: Each expert in llmre.model.moe is a SwiGLU module, the same gated FFN used in modern dense LLaMA-style blocks. The router is a separate bias-free linear layer mapping dim to n_experts.

question: In the MoE route() method, what does probs.topk(self.top_k, dim=-1) return and what is done next?
options: The k smallest probabilities and their indices per token, which are then masked out of the softmax output entirely
A one-hot mask over all N experts per token, which is then passed through a second softmax to form gates
The k largest probabilities and their expert indices per token; the kept gates are then divided by their sum
The k tokens most strongly assigned to each expert, so that each expert processes exactly k tokens per batch
explanation: topk along the expert dimension returns, for each token, the k highest probabilities (gates) and the indices of those experts, each of shape (N_tok, k). The gates are then renormalized by their row sum. It selects experts per token, not tokens per expert.

question: In the from-scratch MoE forward, how is each expert's work restricted to its own tokens?
options: Every expert runs on all tokens, and its output is multiplied by a zero gate wherever it was not selected
Tokens are sorted by expert index and padded to equal length so all experts run as one batched matmul
A boolean mask of tokens that chose the expert gathers a sub-batch; the expert runs once and gated results are added back
Each token is processed in its own Python loop iteration, calling only the experts it selected, one after another in order
explanation: For each expert e, sel = (topk_idx == e) marks which tokens chose it, token_mask = sel.any(-1) selects them, the expert runs once on x_flat[token_mask], and the gate-weighted result is scattered into out. An expert with no tokens is skipped. Running every expert on all tokens would give the same output but no compute saving.

question: In the from-scratch MoE, how is the gate weight for expert e extracted for each token?
options: (topk_gate * sel).sum(dim=-1), which picks the gate in whichever top-k slot held expert e
probs[:, e], the router probability for expert e before the top-k gates are renormalized
topk_gate[:, 0] for every expert, since the first slot always holds the largest gate value
sel.float().mean(dim=-1), the fraction of top-k slots in which expert e was selected
explanation: sel is a (N_tok, k) boolean telling which of a token's k slots chose expert e; multiplying by the renormalized gates and summing over k yields that expert's gate (zero if not chosen). Using probs[:, e] would skip the renormalization.

question: How are shared experts applied in the from-scratch MoE forward?
options: Shared experts are added to the router's candidate list and compete with routed experts for top-k slots
Shared experts run only on the tokens that no routed expert selected, as a fallback path
Shared experts' outputs are averaged together and then multiplied by the routed experts' gates
Each shared expert is run on all tokens and its output is added to the routed output without a gate
explanation: The code loops over self.shared and does out = out + sh(x_flat): every token goes through every shared expert, ungated. That matches the always-on term of the DeepSeekMoE output formula.

question: In the MoE aux loss code, why is f detached in aux = n_experts * torch.sum(f.detach() * P)?
options: Detaching f only saves activation memory; it leaves the gradient with respect to the router weights unchanged
f is a hard token-count fraction; detaching it makes gradients flow only through the soft mean probability P
Detaching f stops the expert FFN weights from being updated by the load-balancing term at all
f must be detached because it is computed on the CPU, while P lives on the GPU with the router
explanation: f is computed from one-hot top-k assignments, which carry no meaningful gradient; treating it as a constant means the loss's gradient comes from P, matching the derivation where the router is nudged through $P_i$. It is not a memory trick, and the expert weights are trained by the LM loss regardless.

question: In the MoE aux loss code, how is the per-expert token fraction f computed?
options: Take the softmax router probabilities and average them over all tokens in the batch, separately for each expert
One-hot encode topk_idx, sum over the k slots to get a (N_tok, N) assignment matrix, then average over tokens
Count the number of nonzero expert outputs per token and divide that count by the hidden size C
Divide each expert's parameter count by the total parameter count summed across all N experts
explanation: F.one_hot(topk_idx, n_experts) has shape (N_tok, k, N); summing over k gives which experts each token used, and the mean over tokens gives the fraction of routed assignments per expert. The mean of probabilities is P, the other factor.

section: 7. Under the hood: verify the routing and the aux loss
question: In an MoE with N experts and top-k routing, what is the per-token compute cost?
options: About N dense-FFN passes, since the router must evaluate every expert
About N/k dense-FFN passes, split evenly across the selected experts
About one dense-FFN pass regardless of k, because the gates sum to 1
About k dense-FFN passes plus a tiny router matmul, independent of N
explanation: Each token runs through its k chosen experts, so cost is roughly k FFN passes, and adding more experts does not raise it. The router's C-by-N matmul is negligible. Using k = 2 costs about twice a single FFN, not one.

section: 7. Under the hood: verify the routing and the aux loss
question: What are the real engineering costs of Mixture of Experts at scale, beyond FLOPs?
options: Memory for all experts, all-to-all traffic to ship tokens to experts on other devices, and load imbalance
Extra attention computation for every expert, because each expert needs its own attention sublayer and KV cache
A KV cache that grows linearly with the number of experts, since each expert caches keys and values
Recomputing the router once per expert in the backward pass, which doubles the cost of every layer
explanation: All N experts must be stored, typically sharded across GPUs with expert parallelism, so tokens are sent via all-to-all to wherever their chosen experts live. That communication plus imbalance from uneven routing are the real costs, which is why load balancing matters so much. Experts do not add attention or KV cache.

section: 7. Under the hood: verify the routing and the aux loss
question: In expert parallelism for Mixture of Experts, how do tokens reach their chosen experts?
options: Every GPU holds a full copy of all experts, so tokens never move and only gradients are all-reduced
Expert weights are streamed from CPU memory to each GPU on demand whenever a token in the local batch selects them
Each GPU holds a subset of experts, and an all-to-all exchange ships tokens to the devices holding their experts
Tokens are broadcast to every GPU, and each GPU runs all its experts and keeps the selected outputs
explanation: Expert parallelism shards experts across devices, so routing requires an all-to-all where each device sends tokens to the device of each chosen expert and receives results back. Replicating all experts everywhere would remove the memory benefit of sharding.

section: 7. Under the hood: verify the routing and the aux loss
question: What is the 'capacity factor' in production MoE training, and what happens to overflow tokens?
options: A minimum number of tokens each expert must receive per batch; shortfalls are padded with zero vectors
A multiplier on each expert's hidden size that grows during training as more tokens are routed to it
A cap on tokens each expert accepts per batch; overflow tokens are dropped and pass only through the residual
A cap on experts per token; whenever the router picks more experts than the cap allows, the extras are averaged
explanation: Production kernels give each expert a fixed buffer per batch. If the router sends more tokens than that, the excess skip the expert and only the residual connection carries them forward. Good balancing keeps drops rare; a collapsed router drops heavily.

section: 7. Under the hood: verify the routing and the aux loss
question: Does the course's teaching MoE implementation enforce an expert capacity limit?
options: No; it runs every routed token, which is fine on CPU but differs from how production kernels behave
Yes; tokens above a capacity factor of 1.25 are dropped and pass through only the residual connection
Yes; overflow tokens are rerouted to their next-best expert, as production MoE kernels do
No; instead it runs every expert on every token and zeroes out the unselected outputs
explanation: The teaching code has no capacity cap, so no token is dropped. Production kernels use fixed per-expert capacity and drop overflow. It still runs only the routed experts per token, not all experts.

question: Which is a correct statement about gradients in MoE training?
options: Gradients should flow through both f_i and the top-k selection, using a straight-through estimator
Only f_i should carry gradient, since P_i is a probability and must be detached to keep it properly normalized
The router receives no gradient at all and stays fixed at its initialization throughout training
Detach the hard count f_i; gradients flow through P_i, and the top-k selection itself is not backpropagated
explanation: f_i is a discrete count and is detached; P_i is the differentiable route by which the aux loss trains the router. The top-k choice is not differentiated. The router also learns from the LM loss through the gate weights.

question: What goes wrong if an MoE implementation forgets to renormalize the top-k gate weights?
options: The router selects the wrong experts, because the top-k operation is then applied to unnormalized logits
The kept probabilities sum to less than 1, so the output is not a proper weighted average of the experts
Load balancing becomes impossible, since the aux loss needs top-k gates that sum to exactly 1 for every token
The aux loss becomes negative, which pushes the router toward collapse instead of balance
explanation: Selecting k of N experts leaves probabilities that sum to less than 1, which scales the output down. Renormalizing makes the gates sum to 1. Selection itself is unaffected; only the blending is wrong.

question: Why should MoE models report both total parameters and active parameters?
options: Total counts the parameters used in training, while active counts only those tied to the tokenizer vocabulary
Total measures memory to store all experts; active measures per-token compute; in MoE they differ greatly
The two are always equal in MoE, but reporting both is a convention inherited from dense model papers
Active parameters measure the memory to store the model, while total parameters measure per-token compute
explanation: For DeepSeek-V3, 671B total sets the memory footprint, while about 37B active per token sets the compute cost. Confusing them misjudges either cost. The tempting reversed option swaps which number governs memory and which governs compute.

question: A dense FFN with P parameters is replaced by an MoE of 8 experts, each the same size as the dense FFN, with top-2 routing (ignore the router). What are total parameters, active parameters per token, and their ratio?
options: 8P total, about 8P active, a 1x ratio
2P total, about P active, giving a 2x ratio
8P total, about P active, an 8x ratio
8P total, about 2P active, a 4x ratio
explanation: Eight experts of size P store 8P parameters; each token runs its top-2, so about 2P are active; 8P / 2P = 4. You get 8 times the FFN capacity at about twice the per-token FFN compute. The 8x option would only hold for top-1.

question: An MoE model's expert 3 processes about 90% of tokens after a few hundred steps, yet LM loss keeps falling. What was most likely forgotten?
options: The auxiliary load-balance loss (or an equivalent balancing mechanism), causing router collapse
The renormalization of the top-k gates, so the kept gate weights no longer sum to 1
The causal attention mask, which lets expert 3 see future tokens and so win nearly every routing choice
Weight decay on the router matrix, which lets one expert's logit grow without any bound
explanation: Without a balancing term, the rich-get-richer loop concentrates tokens on a few experts: router collapse. The fix is to add the aux loss or DeepSeek-V3's bias update. Unnormalized gates would scale outputs but not cause this concentration.

question: Why can the LM loss still go down for a while in an MoE suffering router collapse?
options: A collapsed router produces a lower aux loss, and that drop is added directly into the reported LM loss
The dead experts keep receiving gradient through their gates, so they still improve slowly
The one or two overworked experts still learn, so the model behaves like a much smaller dense model
Router collapse speeds up the attention layers, which lowers loss through faster convergence
explanation: The few experts that receive tokens keep improving, so the model trains like a small dense model and loss falls. But it never uses the capacity it paid for, and on sharded hardware the load is badly imbalanced. Collapse actually raises the aux loss, toward its maximum N.

question: Which papers introduced top-1 routing with the aux loss, fine-grained plus shared experts, and aux-loss-free bias balancing, respectively?
options: DeepSeekMoE; Switch Transformers; Mixtral 8x7B
DeepSeek-V3; DeepSeekMoE; Switch Transformers
Switch Transformers; DeepSeekMoE; DeepSeek-V3
Mixtral; DeepSeek-V3; DeepSeekMoE
explanation: Switch Transformers (Fedus et al. 2021) introduced top-1 routing with the load-balance aux loss; DeepSeekMoE (Dai et al. 2024) added fine-grained and shared experts; DeepSeek-V3 (2024) added aux-loss-free bias balancing and scaled to 671B total / about 37B active. Read in that order, each refines the last.

question: Why is the aux loss $N\sum_i f_i P_i$ minimal when load is uniform, and how does its gradient fix router collapse?
options: Uniform $f_i = P_i = 1/N$ gives the minimum 1; gradient through $P_i$ moves probability off overloaded experts onto idle ones
Uniform routing gives the maximum value N, so its gradient pushes the router to concentrate tokens on one expert to lower it
It is minimal at uniform load because $f_i$ is then zero; the gradient through $f_i$ directly reassigns tokens to experts
Uniform load sets $P_i = 1$ for all experts; its gradient raises the router softmax temperature until routing is random
explanation: The sum of products $f_iP_i$ is smallest when both are spread evenly, giving 1. Because the hard counts are detached, the gradient acts on the router probabilities $P_i$, shifting mass toward under-used experts and spreading load. It does not reassign tokens directly or change a temperature.

question: In DeepSeek-V3's '~37B active parameters per token', which parameters are counted as active?
options: All 671B parameters divided by the number of layers, since a token passes through one layer at a time
Only the router weights in every layer, because those are the only weights that every single token is guaranteed to use
Only the attention weights in every layer; expert FFN weights are excluded because they are sparse
The shared experts plus the top-k routed experts a single token actually flows through, which set its compute cost
explanation: Active parameters are those a single token actually computes with: its always-on shared experts plus its selected top-k routed experts. That sets the per-token compute, while the 671B total sets memory.
